implementation_notes: In async Rust the expiry index is a library type: tokio-util's DelayQueue stores payloads with a deadline (insert(value, timeout) or insert_at(value, Instant)), yields them in deadline order from a timer wheel, is cancellation-safe as a Stream, and hands back a Key so an item consumed in time can be removed before it expires. That replaces a hand-rolled min-heap plus wake-up plumbing, and tokio::time::Instant keeps the comparison monotonic within the runtime. A std-only or synchronous service has no such primitive and falls back to std::time::Instant with a BinaryHeap, polled or drained on a recv_timeout cycle. Because Instant is process-local, the on-the-wire form must be an absolute UTC timestamp that each hop converts once.
pitfalls: tokio::time::Instant only advances when the runtime is polled (and is frozen under paused-time tests); it is process-local, so serializing it produces deadlines that are meaningless to the peer.

DelayQueue yields expired entries but does nothing with them: the consumer must dead-letter rather than process, and must remove(&key) when it handles an item early or the entry lingers until its deadline.

Keeping the payload inside the queue while a handler also owns it fights the borrow checker; the idiomatic shape is to move the value out (into the handler or the dead-letter path) and keep only the Key for cancellation.
